questions.prompt: The spread's z-score is -2.4 and you hold no position. What does the rule do?
options: Short 1 share of A and buy h shares of B
Nothing, because only a z-score above 2 opens a trade
Buy 1 share of A and short h shares of B
questions.explanation: A z-score below -2 means the spread A - h × B is cheap. You buy the spread: long the A leg and short h shares of the B leg, and wait for it to rise back toward its mean.

questions.prompt: In the trade on day 296, both A and B fell in price. Why did the trade still make 0.93 per spread unit?
options: Because the short A leg gained more (1.59) than the long B leg lost (0.66)
Because a pairs trade cannot lose money
Because the hedge ratio was fitted on the same days
Because B's price rose during the trade
questions.explanation: The trade bets on the gap, not on the direction of the market. A fell by more than 1.362 times B's fall, so 1.59 - 0.66 = 0.93.

questions.prompt: Why does the backtest fit the hedge ratio on the first 250 days and trade only the last 250?
options: Because the z-score needs 250 days of data
Because a ratio fitted on every day would use future prices, which is look-ahead bias
Because cointegration only holds in the second half
questions.explanation: A hedge ratio fitted on all 500 days knows prices the trader could not have seen on day 250. Fitting on earlier days only keeps each decision honest.
